prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The gates clanged and they walked you into jail More tense than felons but relieved to find The hostile world shut out, the flags that dripped From every mother’s windowpane, obscene The bloodlust sweating from the public heart, The dog authority slavering at your throat. A sense of quiet, of pulling down the blind Possessed you. Punishment you felt was clean. The decks, the catwalks, and the narrow light Composed a ship. This was a mutinous crew Troubling the captains for plain decencies, A Mayflower brim with pilgrims headed out To establish new theocracies to west, A Noah’s ark coasting the topmost seas Ten miles above the sodomites and fish. These inmates loved the only living doves. Like all men hunted from the world you made A good community, voyaging the storm To no safe Plymouth or green Ararat; Trouble or calm, the men with Bibles prayed, The gaunt politicals construed our hate. The opposite of all armies, you were best Opposing uniformity and yourselves; Prison and personality were your fate. You suffered not so physically but knew Maltreatment, hunger, ennui of the mind. Well might the soldier kissing the hot beach Erupting in his face damn all your kind. Yet you who saved neither yourselves nor us Are equally with those who shed the blood The heroes of our cause. Your conscience is What we come back to in the armistice.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The poem addresses the imprisonment of conscientious objectors during wartime, using vivid carceral, biblical, and nautical imagery to portray jail as both punishment and a refuge from public militaristic hatred. It concludes that although these prisoners did not fight or save others directly, their moral resistance makes them equal heroes whose conscience remains essential after the violence ends.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, More, From

outputs.L1:
The gates clanged shut, and they led you into jail—  
more tense than felons, yet relieved to find  
the hostile world shut out: the flags that dripped  
from every mother’s windowpane, obscene;  
the bloodlust sweating from the public heart;  
the dog of authority slavering at your throat.  

A sense of quiet, of pulling down the blind,  
possessed you. Punishment, you felt, was clean.  
The decks, the catwalks, and the narrow light  
composed a ship. This was a mutinous crew,  
troubling the captains for plain decencies;  
a Mayflower brimmed with pilgrims headed west  
to establish new theocracies;  
a Noah’s ark coasting the topmost seas,  
ten miles above the sodomites and fish.  
These inmates loved the only living doves.  

Like all men hunted from the world, you made  
a good community, voyaging through the storm  
toward no safe Plymouth or green Ararat.  
In trouble or calm, the men with Bibles prayed;  
the gaunt politicals construed our hate.  
The opposite of all armies, you were best  
in opposing uniformity—and yourselves.  
Prison and personality were your fate.  

You suffered not so much physically, but knew  
maltreatment, hunger, and the ennui of the mind.  
Well might the soldier, kissing the hot beach  
erupting in his face, damn all your kind.  
Yet you, who saved neither yourselves nor us,  
are, equally with those who shed the blood,  
the heroes of our cause. Your conscience is  
what we return to in the armistice.
outputs.L2:
The doors slammed shut, and you were led inside the prison. You were more anxious than criminals, yet grateful that the angry outside world had been sealed away: the flags hanging from mothers’ windows, the indecent eagerness for blood in the public mood, and the snarling force of authority pressing against you.

A calm feeling came over you, like lowering a shade. Punishment seemed almost pure. The decks, walkways, and thin shafts of light made the place feel like a ship. Its prisoners were like rebels challenging their commanders for basic human fairness. They seemed like pilgrims on a crowded Mayflower sailing west to found new rigid faiths, or like Noah’s ark drifting above the highest waters, far over the condemned cities and the drowned creatures below. These prisoners cherished the only living signs of peace.

Driven out by the world, you formed a strong community, traveling through turmoil without any promised safe harbor—no Plymouth, no green Ararat. In hardship or in quiet, the men with Bibles prayed, while the thin political prisoners tried to interpret the hatred directed at them. Unlike armies, you were at your finest when resisting sameness, even within yourselves. Prison and individual conscience became your destiny.

Your suffering was not chiefly bodily, but you endured mistreatment, hunger, and the dull exhaustion of the spirit. A soldier landing on a burning beach, with explosions in his face, might understandably curse people like you. Still, though you saved neither yourselves nor the rest of us, you stand alongside those who spilled blood as heroes of our cause. Your conscience is the thing we return to when the fighting ends.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents the jail not simply as a place of punishment, but as a strange refuge from an even more threatening world outside. When the prisoners enter, they feel a kind of relief because the prison walls shut out the hostile, bloodthirsty public that has rejected them. Outside, society appears cruel, vengeful, and eager to condemn; inside, despite confinement, there is at least protection from that violence.

The jail is also imagined as a ship, carrying a small rebellious community away from the corrupt values of the wider world. This image gives the prisoners a sense of shared purpose. They are not merely criminals or victims, but people who have refused to accept the moral standards of society. Like passengers on a difficult voyage, they are united by their desire for decency, justice, and moral meaning.

Within the prison, the inmates form a fragile community of outcasts. Their bond is not easy or secure, because they are isolated, deprived, and constantly under pressure. Yet they continue to resist conformity. Their imprisonment becomes a sign of their refusal to surrender their beliefs, even when society punishes them for standing apart.

Their suffering is shown as largely psychological. They endure maltreatment, hunger, and the deadening boredom of prison life, but the deepest pain comes from mental confinement and emotional strain. The monotony, humiliation, and isolation of jail test their inner strength more than their bodies.

Ultimately, the poem honors the prisoners’ conscience and moral resistance. It suggests that their courage is heroic, even if it is quieter than the courage shown on a battlefield. By comparing their endurance with the sacrifice of those who fought and died in war, the poem gives dignity to their suffering. Their heroism lies in remaining faithful to their principles in the face of cruelty, rejection, and imprisonment.
outputs.L4:
The poem reflects on the imprisonment of conscientious objectors during wartime and presents their refusal to fight as an act of moral courage rather than cowardice. It describes the prison in vivid and often harsh imagery: the barred cells, locked doors, and oppressive atmosphere emphasize the punishment these men endure for obeying their consciences. At the same time, the jail is shown almost paradoxically as a kind of refuge, protecting them from the hatred of a society swept up in militarism and eager to condemn anyone who will not participate in war.

The poem also draws on biblical and nautical imagery to deepen its meaning. The prisoners are associated with spiritual endurance, sacrifice, and faithfulness to a higher moral law, suggesting that their suffering has a religious or prophetic significance. Nautical images evoke the idea of people caught in a storm, isolated from the violent currents of public opinion yet still holding fast to an inner compass. Through these images, the poem portrays conscience as something that can guide human beings even when the surrounding world has lost its moral direction.

By the end, the poem argues that heroism should not be measured only by battlefield action. The conscientious objectors may not have carried weapons, fought enemies, or rescued comrades in the direct, dramatic ways usually celebrated during war. Nevertheless, their refusal to take part in killing represents a different but equally important form of bravery. Their resistance exposes the moral cost of war and preserves a humane vision that will be needed once the violence is over. The poem ultimately honors them as heroes of conscience, insisting that their quiet endurance and principled suffering are as vital as more conventional acts of wartime courage.
outputs.L5:
**The More We Learn From Life**

The more we experience, the more we understand about ourselves and the world around us. Every lesson comes from somewhere: from success, from failure, from kindness, from change, and from the people we meet along the way.

The journey of life is not always simple, but each moment offers something valuable. From challenges, we gain strength. From mistakes, we gain wisdom. From hope, we find the courage to continue.

The more we remain open to learning, the more meaningful our path becomes. Life teaches us that growth often comes from unexpected places, and every new day gives us another chance to become better than we were before.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a mid-20th-century style free verse poem about conscientious objectors in prison during wartime, portraying them as both isolated from and morally central to society.
counterfactuals.output:
In the season of headlines and ration cards,  
when the loudspeakers bloomed in the squares  
and maps were pinned like wounds to every wall,  
they were taken quietly  
to the county prison.

No brass band followed.  
No mothers waved flags at the station.  
Only the iron door,  
the clerk’s cough,  
the inventory of shoelaces, belt, pencil, name.

Outside, the nation marched in columns—  
boots in the rain,  
factory whistles,  
the gray bread of necessity.  
Children learned the names of distant rivers  
because men were dying beside them.  
Women stood in lines for sugar,  
for news,  
for the return of faces.

Inside, they folded blankets.  
They scrubbed the stone floor.  
They listened at night  
to the pipes knocking like code  
through the walls.

They had said no.

A small word,  
unarmed,  
without a uniform,  
without a medal in its future.  
A word thin enough  
to slip under a cell door,  
yet heavy enough  
to stop a train in the mind.

They were called cowards  
by men who had never seen them wake  
before dawn,  
never seen the long obedience  
of refusing hatred  
when hatred was the common weather.

They were called traitors  
though they kept faith  
with the first law  
older than parliaments,  
older than bugles,  
the law written in the body  
when it sees another body fall.

In their cells  
they were far from everything—  
from the warm kitchens,  
the newspapers slapped on porches,  
the dance halls with their dim blue lamps,  
the great engines turning night into metal.

Yet the city moved around them  
as a wheel around its hub.

The judge forgot them at dinner.  
The warden counted them at dusk.  
The minister prayed for victory  
and did not name them.  
But somewhere in the dark machinery  
of the republic  
their silence remained,  
a grain of sand,  
a seed.

They did not stop the war.  
The ships went out.  
The telegrams came in.  
Snow fell on helmets  
and on the barred windows alike.

Still, there they were:  
men without guns  
guarding something  
no arsenal could store,

alone as conscience is alone,  
central as conscience is central,

sitting on their narrow beds  
while the century burned,  
holding in empty hands  
the shape of another world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a serious, literary poem in the voice of someone addressing imprisoned pacifists, using imagery of ships, biblical voyages, public hatred, and wartime conscience.
counterfactuals.output:
To those behind the iron morning,

I have seen your names go under  
like lanterns lowered from a quay,  
while the harbor shouted after you—  
coward, traitor, Judas, fool—  
and the gulls, white as torn proclamations,  
wheeled above the roofs of the nation.

They have locked you where the daylight  
comes in rationed, square by square,  
where footsteps measure out the hours  
and bread arrives without a blessing.  
Yet I think of ships.

Not the proud destroyers shouldering the foam,  
not the gray guns steaming toward a foreign dawn,  
but those frail arks of refusal—  
Noah’s pitched dark, rocking with breath and terror;  
Jonah’s hold, where conscience slept  
and woke to the wet thunder of judgment;  
Paul’s wrecked vessel breaking on the reef,  
men clinging to planks beneath a storm  
that had no respect for empire.

You, too, have sailed.

You crossed the public square  
as over a blackened sea.  
The crowd rose like weather.  
Their mouths were waves against you,  
their flags hard rain,  
their righteous music iron in the blood.  
They loved the war as men love fire  
when winter has entered the bone;  
they fed it sons and hymns and harvests,  
and called its hunger peace.

But you would not kneel  
before the altar of the trumpet.  
You would not dress murder  
in the uniform of duty.  
You stood with empty hands  
while the century demanded weapons,  
and for this the gates closed over you  
with the sound of a verdict hammered shut.

Do not think you are forgotten  
because the newspapers spit your names,  
because ministers bless the marching columns,  
because mothers, made bitter by fear,  
turn their faces from your windows.  
Hatred is also a kind of witness:  
the world knows where the wound is  
and presses there.

In the deep cell of the state  
your silence works like salt.  
It enters the meat of power.  
It keeps alive what would otherwise rot—  
the old commandment,  
the impossible mercy,  
the Christ walking unarmed  
through the armed imagination of man.

O prisoners of the unsheathed age,  
keepers of the word not kill,  
may your nights be crossed by a small sail,  
may a dove beat once against the bars,  
may you hear, beyond the warder’s keys,  
the sea withdrawing from all battlefields.

For every empire launches its ships  
with brass and prayer and cheering,  
but somewhere, always,  
a remnant refuses the voyage.  
Somewhere a conscience, chained and cold,  
becomes the shore  
toward which the drowned world turns.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem resembling 1940s American war poetry, about men jailed for refusing military service and how their moral witness survives after the fighting ends.
counterfactuals.output:
**After the Armistice**

They would not shoulder steel nor learn  
the trade of thunder in the hand;  
so iron doors were made to turn  
and hide them from the marching land.  

Outside, the bugles split the dawn,  
the troop trains vanished in the rain;  
inside, they counted summers gone  
by shadows crossing windowpane.  

Men called them cowards in the street,  
and mothers turned their eyes away;  
yet still they kept, in their defeat,  
a stubborn Sabbath in the day.  

They scrubbed the floors, they broke the bread,  
they wrote their letters straight and plain:  
*We cannot answer dead with dead,  
nor cleanse the earth by adding pain.*  

The war moved on—through smoke and snow,  
past beaches red and cities burned;  
the headlines shouted blow for blow,  
the great wheels of the nation turned.  

Then came the flags, the bells, the cries,  
the boys with medals on their coats,  
the empty sleeves, the hollow eyes,  
the names read out in courthouse notes.  

And from the prisons, one by one,  
the silent men came back to air;  
no brass proclaimed what they had done,  
no wreath was waiting for them there.  

But years, like rivers, wear down stone.  
The anger of the crowd grows thin.  
A child will ask, in gentler tone,  
where peace begins, where wars begin.  

Then someone finds a yellowed page,  
a jailhouse psalm, a witness kept:  
men locked away by their own age  
because they would not kill—or slept  

uneasy while the cannons ceased,  
believing mercy must be tried;  
that victory is not yet peace  
while hatred walks home satisfied.  

So let the drums fall out of tune,  
let old parades go drifting past;  
the quieter courage, late or soon,  
is also counted, and will last.  

For after rifles rust and fade,  
after the bitter fields are green,  
the conscience no command could raid  
stands watch where armies once have been.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a dense modernist poem that compares a wartime prison to a mutinous ship, a Mayflower, and Noah’s ark, ending with a reflection on conscience after armistice?
counterfactuals.output:
**Armistice Hull**

The prison lists in its own weather—  
masonry yawing under searchlights,  
iron bunks stacked like reefs of ribs,  
men sleeping in the bilge of nations.

At night the corridors creak:  
a mutinous ship, no captain but hunger,  
no mast but the rifle’s black arithmetic,  
no compass but the cough passed hand to hand  
through straw, through fever, through the dark  
salt of remembering.

Someone whispers: land.  
Someone laughs: England.  
Someone prays: not again.  
And still we sail—  
our barred Mayflower, cargoed with dissent,  
pilgrims in reverse,  
faith stripped to a tin cup,  
the new world postponed behind wire.

Rain drums the roof: forty days, forty orders.  
The guards count us by pairs,  
unclean, unchosen, yet alive;  
we are Noah’s beasts without the promise,  
snarling, shivering, breeding only rumors,  
while the dove circles and circles  
with no green in its beak.

Then the guns stop.  
The sea withdraws from the blood.  
Doors open like wounds pretending to heal.

Armistice: a word folded white,  
laid on the table between victor and corpse.  
We walk out carrying the jail inside us,  
each man his own tribunal,  
each silence cross-examined.

For after the flags, after the brass bands,  
after history washes its hands in public fountains,  
conscience remains—  
that small, mutinous stowaway—  
asking who was saved,  
who was sacrificed,  
and who, having lived,  
will dare to answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a solemn poem about pacifists or political prisoners during World War II, contrasting soldiers’ sacrifice with the prisoners’ refusal to kill and treating both as heroes of the same cause.
counterfactuals.output:
**Heroes of the Same Dawn**

They went with rifles into smoke,  
through iron rain and broken sky,  
and offered up their breath and youth  
where fields were taught to die.  

Their names were carved in village stone,  
their letters kept, their medals shined;  
they stood between the wolf and door,  
and left their lives behind.  

But in the cells behind the walls,  
where no brass music ever came,  
there knelt the ones who would not kill,  
who bore another flame.  

They faced the court, the sneer, the chain,  
the numbered coat, the warder’s tread;  
they chose the hunger of the just,  
the narrow plank for bed.  

No bugle blessed their watch at dawn,  
no banner wrapped their quiet pain;  
yet still they held, with empty hands,  
a line no hate could gain.  

For some must fight the tyrant’s gun  
when all the world is set aflame,  
and some must answer murder’s call  
by refusing murder’s name.  

The soldier’s grave, the prisoner’s stone,  
are shadowed by one mourning tree;  
one gave his life that others live,  
one kept his soul that all be free.  

So let the same wind speak for both,  
across the years, across the scars:  
the fallen under battle clouds,  
the steadfast under bars.  

Not one alone has borne the cost,  
nor one alone redeemed the night;  
they served one dawn by different roads—  
the sword, the chain, the light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
